QUESTION OF THE WEEK - There were two questions this week.
Following Thursday's wages data, economists have lowered expectations that there will be another interest rate cut.
However, it is not out of the question.

A common theme is that while the wages figures were higher than expected, this did not suggest an imminent inflation blowout, and the inflation and wages outlook could still accommodate another easing.
The two main keys to a cut would be the performance of the real economy in coming months, and the outcome of the unions' 'living wage' claim.

Economists were also asked about their preliminary forecasts for fourth quarter GDP, due March 5. A small rise is expected, and negative growth is not totally out of the question in the quarter. The forecasts are preliminary - there is still plenty of information to be released that could change forecasts.

Expenditure based GDP is expected to be the weakest of the three GDP measures, with weak December quarter retail sales and soft exports seen weighing it down. A rise in employment and wages levels in the quarter is expected to make income-based GDP the strongest measure. The wildcard in the GDP equation is stocks data which will be released on March 3.

HOUSING FINANCE - When economists talk of some emerging signs of life in the economy, one of the areas they point to is the housing sector. Housing finance has fallen in the last two months but the expectation is that approvals rose in December. Optimism improved with the release of the Australian Banking Association numbers on Friday. Those with access to the figures were near the top end of the forecast range.

LABOUR FORCE - A small rise is factored in for January to build on the almost 55,000 increase of the previous three months. While this is a positive, growth in employment is still seen as insufficient to see the unemployment rate break away from the 8.5 percent level it has held around since the middle of 1995. Economists said the underestimation of employment due to a new telephone survey method has thrown some confusion into analysis of the labour market at the end of 1996 and the beginning of 1997. Employment is generally expected to gather strength this year but economists said it may be year-end or 1998 before the jobless rate falls to 8.0 percent and below.
